USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the G20 dinner with Xi to open a time-limited negotiating track, not to raise or cut tariffs tomorrow. Keep Lists 1–3 in place and treat the scheduled January 1, 2019 lift of List 3 from 10% to 25% as a bargaining chip that can be paused only against a dated, enforceable work program on IP, forced tech transfer, industrial subsidies, and market access. Do not roll back existing duties, do not accept purchase pledges as a substitute for structural change, and do not fire the threatened additional ~$267B list while talks are live.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modest, not high or existential. The Section 301 record (22 Mar 2018) correctly identifies Chinese IP/tech-transfer practices as a long-run threat to US technology and the industrial base, and combined Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B after List 3 took effect at 10% on 24 Sep 2018, with China matching on ~$60B. That is leverage, not collapse: US industrial production is still firm (INDPRO 104.07 in Nov), Michigan sentiment remains high at 97.5, and CPI is contained. The costs that keep the reading above zero are concentrated and political: China’s soybean retaliation has cut US sales to China by about 94% through mid-October, beans are being piled on the ground, and the $3.6B aid package covers well under half of local price losses—exactly the farm-belt exposure the +0.5 anchor flags, but not yet a material GDP hit. Financial conditions have tightened around the dispute (VIX +45% over the window to 18.49; Baa yields to 5.28%; broad dollar +4.5%), and oil’s drop to ~$50 plus GM layoff headlines have raised the political cost of another unforced escalation. China is the more stressed party (Q3 GDP 6.5%, slowest since 2009; equity drawdown; yuan pressure), so the terrain still favors extracting concessions rather than absorbing an existential shock. Action should therefore be hold-and-talk, not escalate: the Nov 1 Trump–Xi call already teed up Buenos Aires; Lighthizer has said China’s 142-point list does not change unfair practices; APEC failed to produce a communiqué; and Pence/Kudlow have publicly framed G20 as the decision node, with a possible delay of the Jan 1 25% step if talks start. Escalating tariffs now would likely trigger more farm and consumer-goods retaliation and a List-4 path toward duties on nearly all Chinese exports, raising supply-chain and market risk without a new structural ask on the table. Conceding purchases or rolling back before China tables enforcement and timelines would cash in unused leverage for a May-style truce that already collapsed on 29 May. Negotiate is the stance that keeps pressure on while using the only live leader-level window.
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer case remains the core US interest and is still unmet
US already has ~$250B of China imports under tariff; Jan 1 List-3 step-up to 25% and a threatened extra ~$267B are unused leverage
China Q3 growth at 6.5% and market/FX stress give Washington a stronger hand than a crisis narrative implies
Soybean channel is the clearest US wound: ~94% drop in sales to China, storage overflow, incomplete aid offset, farm-district politics after midterms
US real economy not yet breaking (IP and sentiment still solid) but VIX, credit spreads, and a stronger dollar show tightening financial conditions
G20 Trump-Xi meeting is the live decision node; China’s 142-point offer was judged insufficient; a May-style purchase truce already failed

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR Section 301 report finds China IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable; Trump directs tariffs, WTO case, and investment restrictions.
White House announces US will proceed with Section 301 actions on ~$50B; May purchase-truce collapses.
List 3 takes effect at 10% on ~$200B; China retaliates 5–10% on ~$60B; combined US Section 301 coverage ~$250B.
List 3 scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% on January 1, 2019.
Trump and Xi phone call on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
US industrial production latest 104.0681 (2018-11-01), still slightly up over the window.
Michigan consumer sentiment 97.5 in November — still high, not a confidence collapse.
VIX 18.49 on 2018-11-28, +45% over the window, after an October spike above 25.
Moody’s Baa yield 5.28 on 2018-11-28, up ~46 bp — credit conditions tightening.

Officials float a G20 truce that would delay the Jan 1 hike to 25% and hold off ~$267B more while talks proceed; China’s 142-point list judged insufficient; Kudlow says a deal is possible but Trump is willing to stand on tariffs.
US soybean sales to China down ~94% vs last harvest; beans piled outdoors; $3.6B aid at 82.5 cents/bushel covers less than half of local losses.
China Q3 GDP 6.5% y/y, weakest since early 2009, missing 6.6% consensus; IP 5.8% also missed.
Lighthizer: China has not fundamentally altered unfair practices; APEC failed to issue a communiqué; Pence said strategy will not change until China changes.
